templates.name: Explain (cause, origin, advantage, mechanism, definition, significance)
Introduce or describe to an unfamiliar or new audience
Present or describe to an already familiar audience
Specify or identify a single fact

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The waters off Peru support one of the world’s most productive fisheries, dominated by a small fish called the anchoveta.
• Along this coast, persistent winds blowing toward the equator push warm surface water offshore.
• Colder water from the ocean depths rises to replace it, a process known as coastal upwelling.
• This deep water carries dissolved nutrients, such as nitrates, that accumulate below the sunlit surface layer.
• In sunlight, these nutrients fuel dense blooms of phytoplankton, microscopic organisms at the base of the food web that sustains the anchoveta.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why the waters off Peru support such an abundance of fish. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Off Peru’s coast, persistent winds blowing toward the equator push warm surface water offshore, and colder water from the ocean depths rises to take its place.
Winds that push surface water away from Peru’s shore draw up deep, nutrient-rich water, which nourishes the phytoplankton at the base of the anchoveta’s food web.
Because the water that rises off Peru’s coast is colder than the surface water it replaces, the region offers the cool conditions in which the anchoveta thrives.
The waters off Peru, home to one of the world’s most productive fisheries, are dominated by the anchoveta and are also known for a process called coastal upwelling.
items.explanation: The goal is to explain why the waters off Peru hold so many fish. The notes give a chain: winds “push warm surface water offshore,” colder water “rises to replace it,” this deep water “carries dissolved nutrients,” and the nutrients “fuel dense blooms of phytoplankton, microscopic organisms at the base of the food web that sustains the anchoveta.” Choice B follows the whole chain from the winds to the anchoveta’s food supply.

A.recipe: PART (mechanism without the link to fish)
A.why_wrong: It describes how upwelling happens but never mentions the nutrients or the phytoplankton, so it does not explain why the water supports so many fish.

C.why_wrong: It offers a reason, but the notes never say that cool water helps the anchoveta; they credit the nutrients the deep water carries, which feed the phytoplankton.

D.why_wrong: It names the fishery and coastal upwelling side by side but never says how upwelling leads to an abundance of fish.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (coastal upwelling off Peru and the anchoveta fishery). Real, well-known oceanography; no named people or figures (WAVE.md: no fact-checking for this skill). Band 6 shape: why-goal over a chain of four bullets; distractors are the mechanism without the payoff (PART), a wrong cause (cold water instead of nutrients), and both facts with no link.

band7.why: Target 6. Why-goal over a four-bullet chain; A gives the mechanism without the payoff, C a goal-shaped wrong cause (cool water) the notes never give, D both facts with no link. Wrong options are true-but-incomplete or unsupported rather than ambiguous; a fair strong band 6.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo placed part of the US-Mexico boundary along the Rio Grande.
• Over the following years, the river’s channel gradually migrated southward.
• An 1864 flood shifted the channel farther, stranding roughly 600 acres of formerly Mexican territory, known as El Chamizal, north of the river.
• Both governments asserted sovereignty over El Chamizal for nearly a century.
• Under a 1963 agreement, the United States transferred most of the tract to Mexico.
items.stem: The student wants to make and support a generalization about borders that follow rivers. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: After the Rio Grande migrated southward, roughly 600 acres known as El Chamizal ended up north of the river, and both governments claimed the land for nearly a century.
Borders that follow rivers can give rise to long disputes between neighboring nations.
Floods can change the course of a river, as an 1864 flood on the Rio Grande did.
Because rivers can change course, borders that follow them can become contested, as happened when the shifting Rio Grande stranded El Chamizal north of the river.
items.explanation: The goal has two parts: a general claim about borders that follow rivers and a specific case that supports it. Choice D makes the claim (such borders “can become contested” because rivers change course) and supports it with El Chamizal, “formerly Mexican territory” that the shifting river left “north of the river” and over which “Both governments asserted sovereignty” for “nearly a century.”

A.why_wrong: It reports the El Chamizal case accurately but never draws a general claim about borders that follow rivers.

B.why_wrong: It makes a general claim about river borders but gives no case from the notes to support it.

C.why_wrong: It makes and supports a generalization about rivers and floods, not about borders that follow rivers.

items.notes: Subject: history (El Chamizal, the US-Mexico border dispute caused by the shifting Rio Grande). Real subject known without a search; figures kept to the widely cited ones (about 600 acres, 1864 flood, 1963 settlement). Band 6 shape (622a351d, b0620764): claim-only, support-only and wrong-class distractors.

band7.why: Target 6. Make-and-support generalization in the band-6 shape of 622a351d and b0620764: support-only, claim-only and wrong-class options, all accurate.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Maars and calderas are both volcanic depressions, and both often fill with rainwater or groundwater to form lakes.
• A maar forms when rising magma meets groundwater, which flashes to steam and blasts out a broad, shallow crater.
• Most maars measure less than 2 kilometers in diameter.
• A caldera forms when an eruption empties a volcano’s magma chamber and the unsupported summit collapses into the void.
• Calderas can measure tens of kilometers in diameter.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast the role that water plays in the formation of maars and calderas. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Steam from groundwater blasts out a maar, whereas a caldera forms through collapse, with water filling it, if at all, only afterward.
Groundwater flashing to steam blasts out a maar, whereas a caldera’s summit collapses under the weight of the rainwater or groundwater that fills it.
Most maars measure less than 2 kilometers in diameter, whereas calderas can measure tens of kilometers.
Water drives the formation of both: groundwater blasts out maars, and the steam it produces empties the magma chambers beneath calderas.
items.explanation: The goal is to contrast what water does in forming each depression. In a maar, rising magma meets groundwater, “which flashes to steam and blasts out a broad, shallow crater,” so water creates it. A caldera forms when an eruption empties the magma chamber and “the unsupported summit collapses into the void”; the notes mention water only as something that may later “fill” it to form a lake. Choice A states this contrast.

B.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: water made the cause of the collapse)
B.why_wrong: Its account of the maar is accurate, but the notes say a caldera’s summit collapses because an eruption empties the magma chamber and leaves it “unsupported”; water is mentioned only as something that may later fill the depression “to form lakes,” so it does not cause the collapse.

C.recipe: REL (true difference on the wrong dimension)
C.why_wrong: It accurately contrasts the sizes of maars and calderas, but it says nothing about the role water plays in forming them.

D.why_wrong: The notes say an eruption empties a caldera’s magma chamber; they never say that steam from groundwater does, so water does not drive the formation of both.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (volcanic geology: maars and calderas). Textbook-level real facts, no named people or places. Option fact check: A true and does the goal; B FALSE, goal-shaped (true maar half; water made the cause of the caldera collapse); C true, wrong dimension (size); D FALSE, goal-shaped (steam credited with emptying the chamber). Goal-only solve (without the notes): A, B and D all speak to the role of water. Notes register: 34% of lowercase words past rank 10,000, 5.28 chars per word. Review: B was the exact swap of the key (bullet 2 alone decided A against B); it now keeps the true maar half and makes water the cause of the caldera collapse, so the student must join bullet 1 (water fills both) to bullet 4 (collapse after the chamber empties). Key trimmed below B and D in length.
band7_moves: the compared dimension (the role of water) must be derived: the notes describe each formation process and mention water filling both only as an afterthought
key states a relation the notes never state (water creates one, merely fills the other)
two goal-shaped FALSE options: processes swapped, and a false similarity that credits steam with emptying the chamber
one true difference on the wrong dimension (size), the most tempting accurate option

band7.why: As drafted it read band 6: B was a mirror swap of the key settled by bullet 2 and the key was the longest option. Now two goal-shaped FALSE options (B, D) both credit water with forming the caldera, B differs from the key only in its caldera half and is ruled out only by joining bullet 1 (water fills both, afterward) to bullet 4 (the summit collapses into an emptied chamber); the key states a derived relation (water at most fills a caldera afterward) that no bullet states. Goal names the dimension, as in c34d6bff.

fixes: replaced B (an exact role swap of the key, killed by bullet 2 alone) with a goal-shaped FALSE that keeps the true maar half and makes water the cause of the caldera collapse (needs bullets 1 and 4)
trimmed the key (dropped "heated by rising magma") so it is no longer the longest option
explanation now quotes bullets 2 and 4 word for word

items.subtype: Relative degree from two measures pointing opposite ways
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Borneo, the world’s third-largest island, is politically partitioned among Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
• Borneo has an area of approximately 743,000 km² and a population of roughly 23 million.
• Java, a volcanic island in the Indonesian archipelago, lies south of Borneo across the Java Sea.
• Java has an area of approximately 129,000 km² and a population exceeding 150 million.
• Java is home to more than half of Indonesia’s population.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how densely populated Java is compared with Borneo. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Although Borneo is home to more than half of Indonesia’s population, Java, a much smaller island, is far more densely populated.
Borneo has an area of approximately 743,000 km² and a population of roughly 23 million, and Java has an area of approximately 129,000 km² and a population exceeding 150 million.
Although Java covers less than a fifth of Borneo’s area, it is home to more than six times as many people.
With a population exceeding 150 million, Java has well over 100 million more people than Borneo does.
items.explanation: How densely populated an island is depends on both its population and its area. Java has “an area of approximately 129,000 km²” and “a population exceeding 150 million,” while Borneo has “an area of approximately 743,000 km²” and “a population of roughly 23 million.” Choice C puts the two measures together: Java covers less than a fifth of Borneo’s area (129,000 is about 17% of 743,000) yet has more than six times as many people (150 million is about 6.5 times 23 million), so it is far more densely populated.

A.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: number attached to the wrong island)
A.why_wrong: It reaches the right conclusion, but it gives Borneo a fact that belongs to Java: the notes say “Java is home to more than half of Indonesia’s population,” while Borneo has only “roughly 23 million” people.

B.recipe: LIST (both sets of figures, no relation)
B.why_wrong: It gives each island’s area and population but never compares them, so it does not emphasize how densely populated Java is relative to Borneo.

D.why_wrong: It compares the islands’ populations but leaves out their areas, so it cannot show how densely populated Java is compared with Borneo.

items.notes: Subject: geography and population (Java and Borneo). Real figures rounded from well-known values (Borneo about 743,000 km², about 23 million people; Java about 129,000 km², about 151 million at the 2020 census). Option fact check: A FALSE goal-shaped (Java’s share of Indonesia’s population given to Borneo), B LIST, C key (derived ratios: 129/743 = 0.17, 150/23 = 6.5), D PART (people without area). Goal-only solve: A and C both claim Java is denser; only A uses the goal’s words. Notes register: 15% of lowercase words past rank 10,000, 4.90 chars per word (model 5fa51c86 is plain numbers too).
band7_moves: two measures that point opposite ways (area favors Borneo, population favors Java), as in 5fa51c86
key derives a relation the notes never state (population density) and drops the raw numbers
a goal-shaped FALSE option with the right conclusion and a wrong size fact
a LIST option with every figure and no comparison, and a PART option comparing population alone

band7.why: As drafted it read band 6: only A and C said "densely populated", A died on one glance at bullet 2, and the key echoed the goal. Now the key states two derived ratios and never names density, the one option that echoes the goal is a goal-shaped FALSE whose error is a misattached figure (bullet 5 gives the share to Java), B lists all four figures (LIST, as in 5fa51c86) and D compares people only. Weakness kept: the goal names the derived quantity, so there is no opposite-direction tension to resolve as in 5fa51c86.

fixes: key rewritten from "only a fraction ... several times as many people, making it far more densely populated" (an echo of the goal) to derived ratios: less than a fifth of the area, more than six times the people
A was killed at a glance (called Java the larger island); it now carries the goal’s phrase "far more densely populated" and misattaches Java’s share of Indonesia’s population to Borneo
D reworded (population difference, not the key’s "six times") so it is not the key minus its area clause

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Glaze and rime are forms of ice created when supercooled droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, strike a surface.
• Glaze develops from relatively large droplets, such as those in freezing rain, that spread before freezing.
• Glaze accumulates as a smooth, transparent coating.
• Rime develops from tiny droplets, such as those in freezing fog, that freeze instantly on contact.
• Rime accumulates as a white, feathery coating.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference in the appearance of glaze and rime. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Both glaze and rime are created when supercooled droplets strike a surface and freeze.
Rime, which develops when tiny droplets in freezing fog freeze instantly on contact, accumulates as a white, feathery coating.
Glaze accumulates as a smooth, transparent coating, whereas rime accumulates as a white, feathery one.
Glaze develops from relatively large droplets, such as those in freezing rain, while rime develops from tiny droplets, such as those in freezing fog.
items.explanation: The goal is to contrast how glaze and rime look. The notes say glaze “accumulates as a smooth, transparent coating” and rime “accumulates as a white, feathery coating.” Choice C sets these appearances side by side with “whereas.”

A.why_wrong: It states what glaze and rime have in common, how they are created, rather than a difference in how they look.

B.why_wrong: It describes only rime’s appearance and says nothing about glaze, so no difference is shown.

D.why_wrong: It contrasts the droplets each kind of ice develops from, not the appearance of the ice.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (glaze and rime icing). Real meteorology, no named people (WAVE.md: no fact-checking for this skill).

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ornithologists classify hatchlings according to their level of development at hatching.
• Altricial hatchlings, such as those of songbirds, emerge with closed eyes and little or no down.
• They rely entirely on their parents for food and warmth.
• Precocial hatchlings, such as ducklings, emerge with open eyes and a coat of down.
• Within hours, they can walk and feed independently, though they remain near a parent for protection.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference in how dependent the two kinds of hatchlings are on their parents. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: While altricial hatchlings rely entirely on their parents for food and warmth, precocial hatchlings can walk and feed independently within hours.
Altricial hatchlings emerge with closed eyes and little or no down, whereas precocial hatchlings, such as ducklings, emerge with open eyes and a coat of down.
Within hours of hatching, precocial hatchlings such as ducklings can walk and feed independently.
Ornithologists classify hatchlings, from songbirds to ducklings, according to their level of development at hatching.
items.explanation: The goal is to contrast how dependent the two kinds of hatchlings are. Altricial hatchlings “rely entirely on their parents for food and warmth,” while precocial hatchlings “Within hours ... can walk and feed independently.” Choice A puts the two together with “While.”

B.why_wrong: It contrasts the hatchlings’ eyes and down, not how much they depend on their parents.

C.why_wrong: It describes only precocial hatchlings, so it does not contrast them with altricial ones.

D.why_wrong: It explains how ornithologists classify hatchlings but gives no difference between the two kinds.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (altricial and precocial birds). Real biology, no named people.

items.subtype: One entity against the rest of its category
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Every US state has a legislature, an elected body that makes the state’s laws.
• Forty-nine states divide their legislatures into two chambers, usually a senate and a house of representatives.
• In those states, legislative candidates typically run as members of a political party.
• Nebraska’s legislature, which has met in its current form since 1937, consists of a single chamber.
• Its members are elected on ballots that list no party affiliation.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how Nebraska’s legislature differs from those of other US states. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Since 1937, Nebraska’s legislature has been organized differently from the legislatures of the other US states.
Nebraska’s legislature consists of a single chamber, and its members are elected on ballots that list no party affiliation.
Every US state has a legislature, and most divide theirs into a senate and a house of representatives.
Unlike the other 49 states, which have two-chamber legislatures whose candidates typically run as party members, Nebraska has a single chamber elected without party labels.
items.explanation: The goal is to show how Nebraska’s legislature differs from the others. Forty-nine states “divide their legislatures into two chambers,” and their candidates “typically run as members of a political party,” while Nebraska’s legislature “consists of a single chamber” whose members are elected on ballots that “list no party affiliation.” Choice D sets Nebraska against the other states on both points with “Unlike.”

A.why_wrong: It says Nebraska’s legislature is organized differently but never says in what way.

B.why_wrong: It describes Nebraska’s legislature but never mentions the other states, so no difference is drawn.

C.why_wrong: It describes state legislatures in general and never mentions Nebraska.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Nebraska’s unicameral, nonpartisan legislature). Real civics known without a search.

items.subtype: Explain a process to an unfamiliar audience
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Mokume-gane is a metalworking technique that originated in seventeenth-century Japan.
• Its name translates as “wood-grain metal.”
• Artisans fuse thin sheets of differently colored metals, such as copper and silver, into a layered block.
• They then carve into the block and hammer it flat, exposing the layers in swirling patterns resembling wood grain.
• Originally used to decorate sword fittings, the technique is now popular in jewelry.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how mokume-gane patterns are made to an audience unfamiliar with the technique. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: After fusing the metal sheets into a block, artisans carve into it and hammer it flat, exposing the layers in swirling patterns.
In mokume-gane, a Japanese metalworking technique, artisans fuse sheets of differently colored metals into a block, then carve and flatten it to reveal patterns resembling wood grain.
Originating in seventeenth-century Japan, mokume-gane was first used to decorate sword fittings and is now popular in jewelry.
Mokume-gane, whose name translates as “wood-grain metal,” is a technique in which artisans fuse thin sheets of copper, silver, and other metals.
items.explanation: An unfamiliar audience needs to learn what mokume-gane is as well as how its patterns are made. Choice B identifies it as “a metalworking technique” from Japan and then gives the process: artisans “fuse thin sheets of differently colored metals,” then “carve into the block and hammer it flat,” exposing “swirling patterns resembling wood grain.”

A.why_wrong: It describes the process but never says what technique it belongs to, which an audience unfamiliar with mokume-gane would need.

C.why_wrong: It introduces the technique’s history and uses but does not explain how its patterns are made.

D.why_wrong: It names the technique and its first step but leaves out the carving and flattening that produce the patterns.

items.notes: Subject: arts (mokume-gane metalwork). Real technique known without a search; no named artisans.

items.subtype: Introduce a concept to a new audience
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Cohousing is a type of community in which residents own private homes clustered around shared facilities.
• These facilities typically include a common house with a large kitchen and dining room.
• Residents share meals there several times a week and manage the community collectively.
• The first cohousing communities were built in Denmark in the early 1970s.
• The first American example opened in Davis, California, in 1991.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce cohousing to a new audience. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Cohousing is a type of community in which residents own private homes but share facilities such as a common house, where they eat meals together several times a week.
The first cohousing communities were built in Denmark in the early 1970s, and the first American example opened in Davis, California, in 1991.
In a cohousing community, the common house typically includes a large kitchen and dining room, where residents share meals.
Residents of cohousing communities manage their communities collectively.
items.explanation: A new audience first needs to know what cohousing is. Choice A defines it as “a type of community in which residents own private homes” around “shared facilities” and adds what those facilities are for: residents “share meals there several times a week.”

B.why_wrong: It gives the history of cohousing but never explains what cohousing is.

C.why_wrong: It describes the common house as if the audience already knew what a cohousing community is.

D.why_wrong: It mentions only collective management and does not explain the private homes and shared facilities that define cohousing.

items.notes: Subject: social science (cohousing). Real facts known without a search: Danish origins around 1972, first US community (Muir Commons) in Davis, California, 1991.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ferdinand Cheval (1836–1924) was a rural mail carrier in southeastern France.
• In 1879, he tripped over an unusual stone and began collecting stones along his route.
• With these stones, lime, and cement, he constructed an elaborate structure, the Palais Idéal.
• Working mostly alone in his spare time, he spent 33 years on the project, completing it in 1912.
• In 1969, the French government designated the Palais Idéal a historic monument.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the effort Cheval devoted to building the Palais Idéal. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Cheval, a rural mail carrier in southeastern France, constructed the Palais Idéal from stones, lime, and cement.
In 1969, the French government designated the Palais Idéal, which Cheval had completed in 1912, a historic monument.
Cheval was inspired to build the Palais Idéal after tripping over an unusual stone on his route in 1879.
Working mostly alone in his spare time, Cheval spent 33 years constructing the Palais Idéal.
items.explanation: The goal is to stress how much effort the project took. The notes say that, “Working mostly alone in his spare time, he spent 33 years on the project.” Choice D foregrounds exactly this: decades of solitary work.

A.why_wrong: It says who Cheval was and what he built with but says nothing about how much time or work the project took.

B.why_wrong: It reports the 1969 designation, which shows how the building was later valued, not the effort Cheval put into it.

C.why_wrong: It explains what inspired the project rather than how much effort Cheval devoted to it.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Ferdinand Cheval’s Palais Idéal, Hauterives). Real subject known without a search (built 1879 to 1912, listed as a historic monument in 1969).

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Grand Trunk Road is among the oldest and longest highways in Asia.
• Versions of the route have been traveled for over two millennia.
• In the 1500s, the ruler Sher Shah Suri rebuilt the road and added rest houses at regular intervals.
• Today, it stretches from eastern Bangladesh across northern India and Pakistan to Kabul, Afghanistan.
• Rudyard Kipling’s 1901 novel Kim describes the road as “a river of life.”
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how far the Grand Trunk Road extends. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Versions of the Grand Trunk Road, one of Asia’s oldest highways, have been traveled for over two millennia.
Stretching from eastern Bangladesh across northern India and Pakistan to Kabul, Afghanistan, the Grand Trunk Road crosses four countries.
In the 1500s, Sher Shah Suri rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road and added rest houses at regular intervals.
In his 1901 novel Kim, Rudyard Kipling called the Grand Trunk Road “a river of life.”
items.explanation: The goal is to stress the road’s reach. The notes say it “stretches from eastern Bangladesh across northern India and Pakistan to Kabul, Afghanistan.” Choice B gives that route and adds that it crosses four countries.

A.why_wrong: It emphasizes how long the route has been traveled, not how far it extends.

C.why_wrong: It describes Sher Shah Suri’s work on the road but does not say how far the road runs.

D.why_wrong: It quotes Kipling’s description of the road, which says nothing about its extent.

items.notes: Subject: history (the Grand Trunk Road). Real subject known without a search; no length figure given because published lengths vary; Kipling’s phrase “river of life” is from Kim (1901).

review.note: Kipling quote checked: Kim (Gutenberg #2226) has "such a river of life as nowhere else exists in the world" of the Grand Trunk Road

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A foehn is a warm, dry wind descending the leeward, or sheltered, side of a mountain range.
• A foehn can raise temperatures in Alpine valleys by more than 10°C within hours.
• Moist air ascending the windward slopes cools and loses much of its moisture as precipitation.
• The drier air then descends the opposite slopes.
• During its descent, the air is compressed, which raises its temperature.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why a foehn is warm and dry. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: A foehn, which descends the leeward side of a mountain range, can raise temperatures in Alpine valleys by more than 10°C within hours.
Moist air ascending the windward slopes of a mountain range cools and loses much of its moisture as precipitation.
Having lost much of its moisture as precipitation on the windward slopes, the air in a foehn is compressed and warmed as it descends.
A foehn is a warm, dry wind, and the air that forms it rises up one side of a mountain range and descends the other.
items.explanation: The goal has two parts: why the wind is dry and why it is warm. The notes explain that air ascending the windward slopes “loses much of its moisture as precipitation” and that during its descent “the air is compressed, which raises its temperature.” Choice C gives both causes.

A.why_wrong: It describes what a foehn can do to valley temperatures but not why the wind is warm and dry.

B.why_wrong: It explains how the air loses moisture but never mentions the foehn or why the wind is warm.

D.why_wrong: It states that a foehn is warm and dry and describes the air’s path, but it never explains how that path makes the air warm and dry.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (foehn winds). Real meteorology known without a search; the 10°C figure is a typical, rounded value.

items.subtype: Explain the origin of a name
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Rio de Janeiro is a major metropolis on Brazil’s southeastern coast.
• It borders Guanabara Bay, an expansive inlet of the Atlantic Ocean.
• Portuguese navigators first entered the bay in January 1502.
• Mistaking the bay’s narrow entrance for a river’s mouth, they named the location Rio de Janeiro.
• In Portuguese, the name translates as “River of January.”
items.stem: The student wants to explain the origin of the name Rio de Janeiro. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Rio de Janeiro (“River of January”) was named by Portuguese navigators who entered Guanabara Bay in January 1502, mistaking it for a river’s mouth.
In Portuguese, the name of the Brazilian metropolis Rio de Janeiro translates as “River of January.”
Rio de Janeiro, a major metropolis on Brazil’s southeastern coast, borders Guanabara Bay, an expansive inlet of the Atlantic Ocean.
Portuguese navigators first entered Guanabara Bay, the site of present-day Rio de Janeiro, in January 1502.
items.explanation: To explain the name’s origin, a sentence must say who named the place and why. The navigators arrived “in January 1502” and, “Mistaking the bay’s narrow entrance for a river’s mouth, they named the location Rio de Janeiro,” which translates as “River of January.” Choice A connects all three.

B.why_wrong: It translates the name but does not explain how or why the place came to be called that.

C.why_wrong: It describes where the metropolis is but says nothing about its name.

D.why_wrong: It gives the month the navigators arrived but never connects that date, or their mistake about a river, to the name.

items.notes: Subject: history (how Rio de Janeiro got its name). Real, widely known account.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Pseudocereals are plants outside the grass family whose seeds are prepared and consumed like grains.
• Quinoa was domesticated thousands of years ago in the Andes Mountains.
• Quinoa is a pseudocereal related to spinach and beets.
• Amaranth was a staple crop of the Aztec civilization in present-day Mexico.
• Amaranth is a pseudocereal whose tiny seeds can be boiled or popped.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between quinoa and amaranth. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

Quinoa, a pseudocereal related to spinach and beets, was domesticated thousands of years ago in the Andes Mountains.
Amaranth, a staple crop of the Aztec civilization, has tiny seeds that can be boiled or popped.

A.why_wrong: It contrasts where the two crops come from, a difference rather than a similarity.

items.notes: Subject: natural science and agriculture (quinoa and amaranth). Real facts known without a search.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Chautauqua movement brought lectures, concerts, and other educational programs to American adults.
• It began in 1874 with a summer assembly for Sunday school teachers at Chautauqua Lake, New York.
• That assembly became a permanent institution that still operates today.
• Traveling “circuit Chautauquas,” which pitched tents in small towns for several days, began in 1904.
• By the 1920s, circuit Chautauquas reached millions of people annually.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the order in which the two forms of Chautauqua began. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Before the first summer assembly was held at Chautauqua Lake, traveling circuit Chautauquas had already begun pitching tents in small towns.
Three decades after the first Chautauqua assembly met at Chautauqua Lake, traveling circuit Chautauquas began pitching tents in small towns.
By the 1920s, circuit Chautauquas, which pitched tents in small towns for several days, reached millions of people annually.
The Chautauqua movement, which began with a summer assembly for Sunday school teachers, brought educational programs to American adults.
items.explanation: The assembly at Chautauqua Lake began “in 1874,” and circuit Chautauquas “began in 1904,” thirty years later. Choice B states that order with “Three decades after.”

A.why_wrong: It puts the circuit Chautauquas first, but they began in 1904, thirty years after the 1874 assembly.

C.why_wrong: It describes how many people the circuits reached, not when they began relative to the first assembly.

D.why_wrong: It describes how the movement began and what it offered but never mentions the circuit Chautauquas, so it gives no order.

items.notes: Subject: history (the Chautauqua movement). Real dates known without a search (assembly 1874, circuit Chautauquas from 1904).

A.why_wrong: It describes La verbena de la Paloma but never says it is a zarzuela or explains what zarzuela is.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Sounds above about 20 kilohertz (kHz), the upper limit of human hearing, are called ultrasonic.
• Philippine tarsiers are small primates that often open their mouths as if calling but seem silent.
• Researchers wondered if these primates were communicating at frequencies too high for humans to hear.
• The researchers recorded wild tarsiers with ultrasonic detectors and tested the animals’ hearing.
• The tarsiers’ calls centered on about 70 kHz, and their hearing extended even higher.
items.stem: The student wants to present the study’s results. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The researchers found that Philippine tarsiers call at about 70 kHz, far above the upper limit of human hearing, and can hear even higher frequencies.
Researchers wanted to determine whether Philippine tarsiers, small primates that often open their mouths as if calling, were communicating at frequencies humans cannot hear.
Researchers used ultrasonic detectors to record wild Philippine tarsiers and tested the animals’ hearing.
Sound frequencies above about 20 kHz, the upper limit of human hearing, are known as ultrasonic frequencies.
items.explanation: The results are what the team found: the tarsiers’ calls “centered on about 70 kHz, and their hearing extended even higher,” far above the roughly 20 kHz limit of human hearing. Choice A reports these results.

B.why_wrong: It states what the researchers set out to learn, not what they found.

C.why_wrong: It describes how the researchers gathered data, not what the data showed.

D.why_wrong: It defines ultrasonic frequencies, background to the study rather than its results.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Philippine tarsiers and ultrasound). Real study described generically with an unnamed team; the 70 kHz figure is the one reported for the tarsiers’ calls. No invented figures.

items.subtype: Present findings to a familiar audience
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A nunatak is a mountain peak protruding through an ice sheet, leaving bare rock exposed above the ice.
• Some biologists suspect that plants survived past ice ages on nunataks.
• A team of botanists surveyed 14 nunataks rising above the Greenland ice sheet.
• The team recorded 31 species of flowering plants on the highest of them.
• Nunataks located farther from the ice sheet’s edge supported fewer species.
items.stem: The student wants to present the study’s findings to an audience already familiar with nunataks. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Botanists surveying 14 nunataks, mountain peaks protruding through an ice sheet, recorded 31 flowering plant species on the highest and found fewer species on peaks farther from the ice sheet’s edge.
Some biologists suspect that during past ice ages, plants survived on nunataks.
A nunatak is a mountain peak protruding through an ice sheet, leaving bare rock on which flowering plants can grow.
On 14 nunataks above the Greenland ice sheet, botanists recorded 31 flowering plant species on the highest peak and found fewer species on peaks farther from the ice sheet’s edge.
items.explanation: An audience already familiar with nunataks needs no definition, only the findings. Choice D uses “nunataks” without explaining it and reports both findings: the team “recorded 31 species of flowering plants on the highest of them,” and “Nunataks located farther from the ice sheet’s edge supported fewer species.”

A.why_wrong: It reports the findings but stops to define nunataks, which this audience already knows.

B.why_wrong: It gives an idea some biologists hold, not the findings of the survey.

C.why_wrong: It defines a nunatak, which the audience already knows, and reports none of the study’s findings.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (plants on nunataks). Unnamed, plainly generic survey; the counts (14 nunataks, 31 species) are invented and attached to no real study (WAVE.md wave-3 lesson).

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hutongs are narrow alleys lined with traditional courtyard homes, or siheyuan, in Beijing’s older districts.
• Many hutong neighborhoods have been demolished for high-rise development.
• Architect Qiao Lanxin renovates siheyuan for families who wish to stay in their neighborhoods.
• She keeps each courtyard open to the sky rather than roofing it over for extra indoor space.
• “The courtyard is where a family meets the weather, the seasons, and one another,” she explains.
• She calls her work “a matter of small repairs, not grand gestures.”
items.stem: The student wants to use a quotation from Qiao to explain why she keeps the courtyards open. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Qiao, an architect who renovates siheyuan in Beijing, keeps each home’s courtyard open to the sky rather than roofing it over for extra indoor space.
Qiao leaves each courtyard open because, in her words, the courtyard is “where a family meets the weather, the seasons, and one another.”
Describing her renovations of Beijing’s siheyuan, Qiao calls her work “a matter of small repairs, not grand gestures.”
Many of Beijing’s hutong neighborhoods, lined with traditional siheyuan, have been demolished for high-rise development.
items.explanation: The goal asks for a quotation that explains why Qiao keeps the courtyards open. Choice B quotes her reason: the courtyard is “where a family meets the weather, the seasons, and one another.”

A.why_wrong: It says what Qiao does with the courtyards but gives no quotation and no reason.

C.why_wrong: It quotes Qiao, but the quotation describes her approach in general, not why she keeps the courtyards open.

D.why_wrong: It describes the loss of hutong neighborhoods and contains no quotation from Qiao.

items.notes: Subject: arts and architecture (Beijing hutongs and siheyuan). Qiao Lanxin is an invented architect and her quotations are invented (WAVE.md: invented names where unverified); the name returned no Wikipedia hits.

review.note: invented architect Qiao Lanxin: web search finds no real architect of that name

A pair of hammerkops builds a domed nest out of sticks, mud, and grass.
